newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Bougainville rebel leader blames Chan for crisis.
newsitem.headline: Bougainville rebel leader blames Chan for crisis.

text.p: The leader of an independence uprising on Papua New Guinea's Bougainville island blamed PNG Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan on Tuesday for the crisis which has rocked his government.

Bougainville Revolutionary Army (BRA) political leader Francis Ona said Chan had continually put pressure on the Papua New Guinea defence force to take firmer action against the BRA, which has waged a nine-year war for independence.
"All along, the prime minister of PNG has been pushing the PNG Defence Force, who have already lost the war on Bougainville," Ona told Australian Broadcasting Corporation television.

Chan on Monday sacked his defence force chief Brigadier-General Jerry Singirok after the army head called on the prime minister to resign over the hiring of mercenaries to help end the uprising on Bougainville.
Singirok had said the use of mercenaries called into question the sovereignty and credibility of his troops.

Ona, president of the rebels' self-declared Bougainville Interim Government, said he had no plans to re-open talks to end the rebellion on the resource-rich island, 800 km (500 miles) north-east of Port Moresby.
"I am not for negotiation, I am straight out for independence," he said. "Negotiations will never get us anywhere," he said.

Ona said he believed Chan's recent efforts to end the Bougainville fighting, including the hiring of about 40 foreign mercenaries from British-based Sandline International, were intended to open the island for mining.
"There are five mining companies ready to be set up on the island which means total wipe-out of the all the environment on Bougainville," Ona said.

"The only solution I would see is for the total withdrawal of PNG forces from the island...and for some kind of mechanism so that Bougainvilleans can decide for themselves the political future of Bougainville," he said.
Guerrillas on the island have been fighting Papua New Guinea troops since 1988 after landowners demanded greater compensation for damage caused by the open-cut Panguna copper mine.
The dispute flared into a secessionist uprising that closed the mine the following year and has claimed thousands of lives through fighting or disease.
